# the contributor audit: density selection and geometric defect groups

The exact OC statement remains unproved. This note records a mathematical
audit of the new inputs, not an audit of a complete OC proof.

Continuation: the variable-density theorem's envelope may be imposed
only on Borel sets of full input marginal measure, and its target density
may be infinite on a reference-null set. The reconstructed endpoints
belong to those full-measure sets almost surely. Slice absolute continuity
is proved before the target envelope is applied, so an infinite-density
null set cannot carry output mass. These extensions are useful when the
target density is represented by upper ball averages rather than an
unproved continuous representative. They do not change the compact
supports or the fixed finite target measure in the selection argument.

## 1. Continuous and mixed barycentric selection

Read the continuous proof, its independent density-adversary audit, the
complete mixed extension, and the independent mixed audit. The mechanism
passes with its stated unrestricted Cartesian-product coupling domain.

The important order of arguments is: compact surplus dual attainment;
separate global strongly convex transforms; endpoint reconstruction from
the barycenter; intrinsic absolute continuity by the area formula; then
derivatives on density points of the equality strata. In particular, the
mixed proof does not differentiate ambient Hessians on a prescribed null
slice. The pullback identity proves symmetry intrinsically, and discrete
base derivatives vanish only after slice absolute continuity is known.

The common positive matrix identity gives the exact continuous exponent
d. The finite-dimensional separation uses nonnegative coefficients, so a
positive combination of the finitely many test functions remains convex.
Compact finite intersections then yield one coupling for all convex tests.
This is a selection above one prescribed old law, not a greatest law in
convex order. For d=0, endpoint reconstruction gives the atom bound
directly. These distinctions are essential.

For integer midpoint output across several parity classes, the sharp
ceiling one is false. The example with input bases {0,1}^n and {1,2}^n
forces all admissible midpoint bases to be the all-ones vector. Unit
fiber densities on a common volume-one convex body then force density
at least 2^n. This is a capacity obstruction to a strengthening of the
selection theorem, not a counterexample to OC.

## 2. Polytopal boundary application

Read the complete arbitrary-dimensional polytopal boundary repair note.
For three fibers at bases -1,0,1, the source martingale forces equal
endpoint crossflow masses at each middle source. Tightness of the support
height follows by taking the mean against the preserved normal. Positive
crossflow at a polytopal normal therefore uses three actual parallel
facets, so the continuous density selection theorem applies in dimension
d-1. Convex-order domination permits rebuilding the middle martingale;
disintegration over the selected midpoint restores exactly the original
physical endpoint crossflows. This reconstruction is necessary, since a
new global endpoint pairing alone would not preserve the old source law.

The one selected pairing proves the literal closed-cap inequality by
the affine midpoint identity. Its density ceiling yields the residual
capacity bound, with the strict complement of a closed cap. Neither step
turns convex order into an inequality of source halfspace masses. The
square calculation gives an exact failure of the proposed latter
inequality: 195/38 > 189/38. It is not a critical OC cap law.

The polytopal restriction is material. On a three-dimensional cone the
conditional lateral area on a generator is 2r dr, not its uniform length
measure. No general-body boundary repair follows just by integrating
the facet argument over normals.

## 3. Geometric group flux and normal rigidity

Read the group theorem, including its full rate-zero tail argument, and
the independent optimal-midpoint audit. The proof uses actual cells of a
finite affine minimum. Between distinct limiting zero-plane groups,
transverse coarea or a positive parameter floor gives logarithmic uniform
integrability. Interfaces within a group cancel as geometric interfaces.
Neither property is available for arbitrary source-row allocations.

Boundary coarea away from normals parallel to the affine gradient gives
uniform logarithmic tails. The common interior ball excludes the positive
parallel normal. Thus a group's full zero-set logarithmic defect, even at
rate zero, has its unique negative-gradient normal. The constant radial
weight then turns vector flux into a positive scalar identity.

For the zeroth moment the tail test must precede removing the ordinary
terms: first pass j to infinity at a fixed threshold avoiding inverse
measure atoms, then send the threshold to infinity. Its continuous
coefficient is one at zero, so rate-zero defects remain. Positive-degree
moments plus this zeroth moment identify the full uniform-rate kernel.

Two explicit clarifications from the independent audit are accepted:
state the nontrivial result for d>=2, treating d=1 by the reciprocal-mass
argument that forces a positive parameter floor; and extend the tail
coefficient continuously by one to negative arguments when using uniform
composition on the ambient compact set. The source author is applying
both clarifications.

## 4. Remaining interface

There are now two distinct tools: an exact density-controlled replacement
of barycentric laws, and legitimate geometric conditioning of logarithmic
defects. Neither supplies a single mixed-integer point of the required
depth. In particular, a self-coupling can always be repaired by the
diagonal coupling, so a useful OC application requires an additional
geometric constraint that survives the repair. Likewise normal rigidity
does not separate groups sharing a normal, and cannot justify an
unrestricted source-label-conditioned variational inequality.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
